clue.text: Aplomb — or kind of a trick?

definitions.note: The second definition names the answer as the word that labels a kind of trick rather than as a trick itself; the compound does the work.
definitions.meaning: Self-possession, the composure of somebody who knows exactly what they are doing.
The swindle that works by first winning the victim's trust, then taking the money.

explanation.walkthrough: One word with a respectable sense and a criminal one, and the dash is all that separates them. The trick is the con artist's, sold on trust rather than sleight of hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Confidence is aplomb, poise under pressure; it also names the confidence trick, the fraud that depends on the mark's trust.

clue.text: Prune extract

definitions.note: The first definition is a verb and the second a noun; one spelling serves both readings without changing shape.
definitions.meaning: To cut a hedge or a beard back with shears.
A short piece lifted out of a film or a recording and shown on its own.

explanation.surface: A bottled concentrate made from dried plums.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a phrase, 'prune extract' is something in a health-food aisle, and that reading hides the join between two separate definitions. The second is the film editor's noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To clip is to prune, cutting growth back; and a clip is an extract taken out of a longer piece of film.

clue.text: Heavily armed and dim — peacekeepers flipping!

indicators.note: Something flipping is turned over, so the letters it applies to come back the other way round.

parts.note: Dim is UNCLEAR, so once its opening UN has been flipped the CLEAR behind it stands untouched.
The peacekeepers are the UN, the United Nations, and flipping turns the pair round.

explanation.surface: Soldiers both heavily armed and slow-witted, while the peacekeepers lose their tempers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping!' reads as exasperation, which is what hides the instruction. Dim supplies a seven-letter word that happens to open with the peacekeepers, so only those two letters move.
explanation.definitionFit: A state described as nuclear is armed with atomic weapons, the heaviest armament there is.

clue.text: At home, Mark supposing that Everyman is able to take time to be petty

parts.note: Somebody at home is in.
A mark left on something is a sign of it.
If is the word that introduces a supposition.
The setter of this puzzle signs himself Everyman, so he is I.
Can is the verb for being able.
T is the standard abbreviation for time.

explanation.surface: At home with Mark, who assumes the setter has a moment to spare for small-mindedness.
explanation.walkthrough: Six pieces arrive in the order the clue gives them, which is rare over thirteen letters. Everyman is one of the few setters who names himself in his own clues, and there he is worth one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something insignificant is petty: too small to weigh in whatever is being decided.

clue.text: Fright being topless, a mistake

indicators.note: Being topless is being without a top, and the top of a down entry is the letter at its head.

parts.note: A fright is a terror.
The letter standing at the head of TERROR, and the one that goes.

explanation.surface: A scare caught with its top off, which was a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the top is the first letter, so the loss comes off the front rather than the end. Everyman keeps the cheeky sense of topless in play while doing something quite dry with it.
explanation.definitionFit: An error is a mistake — a slip in a sum, a statement or a piece of work.

clue.text: Chair reupholstered with lamé fabric

indicators.note: Reupholstering strips a covering off and puts the same material back in a different arrangement, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: Five of the nine letters.
The shiny metallic cloth, its accent dropped, supplies the other four.

explanation.surface: An armchair given a new covering in shimmering lamé.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabric' sits at the end looking like part of the furniture and is the definition. Camel hair is cloth woven from the soft undercoat the animal sheds each summer.
explanation.definitionFit: Camel hair is the fabric woven from a camel's soft underwool, best known in overcoats.

clue.text: 4, whichever way you look at it!

indicators.text: whichever way you look at it
indicators.note: a word that is the same whichever way you look at it reads the same forwards and backwards

parts.note: a cross-reference to 4 Down, whose answer is error; a four-letter slang word for a blunder fits

explanation.surface: An exclamation that something is wrong from every angle.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cross-reference: 4 Down is ERROR, and the answer is a slang word for an error that is also a palindrome.
explanation.definitionFit: Boob is British slang for a silly mistake, a synonym of error.

clue.text: Crossword setter's into dictionary, mate: that's kind of complex

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective and the definition a noun phrase: it names the kind of complex the word labels.

indicators.note: Into puts one thing inside another, so the letter it governs is dropped in among the letters around it.

parts.note: The OED is the Oxford English Dictionary, the reference cryptics lean on.
A mate is a pal.
A setter writing about himself is I.

explanation.surface: A setter buried in the dictionary, telling a friend how complicated the job is.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'complex' at the end is Freud's, not the setter's difficulty — that switch is where the clue hides. Everyman referring to himself is worth a single I, and the dictionary is the usual three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oedipus complex is Freud's name for a boy's desire for his mother, and Oedipal is the adjective that labels it.

clue.text: Where you might get a flat top — hopefully not from the tenor

definitions.text: Where you might get a flat top
definitions.meaning: The surface offers a haircut: a flat top is the squared-off crop you ask for in the chair.
The second reading is musical: the close-harmony quartet carries a tenor, and a flat note from him would wreck the chord.

explanation.surface: Somewhere offering a flat-top haircut, with a nervous eye on the tenor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' does two jobs at once — the shape of the crop and a note sung under pitch — and the tenor is there to sing it. Haircuts and four-part harmony share one name.
explanation.definitionFit: A barbershop is where a flat top is cut, and a barbershop quartet is the unaccompanied four-part singing in which a flat tenor ruins everything.

clue.text: Cutter between Channel Islands, losing direction, distressed

parts.note: something in between is in, so between gives the word in

indicators.note: losing means without, so one letter is taken away

parts.note: sore means upset or distressed
E for east, a compass direction

explanation.surface: A boat cutting between Jersey and Guernsey has lost its bearings and is in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The Channel Islands lie off Normandy and include Jersey and Guernsey. 'Losing direction' takes E (east) from SORE, giving SOR.
explanation.definitionFit: An incisor is a front tooth with a sharp edge, used for cutting food.

clue.text: Bullfighter Damon shown exit, we hear

indicators.note: We hear asks for the sound of the words rather than their spelling, so say the fragment aloud and write down what you get.

parts.note: Damon is the film actor Matt Damon, and to be shown a door is to be shown the way out; spoken, the three words run together.

explanation.surface: Somebody called Damon being thrown out, by the sound of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surname is there for the first name, a habit worth knowing: Damon means Matt. 'Shown exit' is the idiom shown the door with its article kept for the extra letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The matador is the bullfighter who leads the final act of a corrida and kills the bull.

clue.text: They go up and down in tailspin, storm raging

definitions.note: The definition describes the answer instead of replacing it: a sentence about what these people do rather than a noun to swap in.

indicators.note: Something raging is violently disordered, and letters caught up in it come out in another arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.surface: Something rising and falling inside a plane's tailspin while a storm rages.
explanation.walkthrough: The two fodder words are the only concrete nouns in a sentence about weather and aircraft, which is why they read as scenery rather than letters. 'They go up and down' describes the people instead of naming them.
explanation.definitionFit: Trampolinists spend their whole sport bouncing up and down off the bed, which is all the definition claims.

clue.text: 'Paella?' groaned displaced American writer

indicators.note: Something displaced has been shifted out of its proper place, and so has every letter here.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.surface: A diner groaning at the suggestion of a Spanish rice dish.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'Paella?' look like reported speech rather than material to shuffle. Poe's full name runs to exactly the thirteen letters the two words hold.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgar Allan Poe was the American writer of Gothic tales and 'The Raven', and the first of the detective story.

clue.text: Somewhat extrovert, he topes too much

indicators.note: Somewhat means partly, so only a part of the words that follow is wanted — the part running straight through them.

parts.note: The run starts four letters into 'extrovert' and carries on unbroken through the two words behind it, stopping two letters short of the end.

explanation.surface: A fairly outgoing man who drinks a great deal more than he should.
explanation.walkthrough: To tope is to drink habitually, an old word Everyman keeps in circulation. The hidden run straddles three words and starts four letters into the first, which is why the join stays invisible.
explanation.definitionFit: Something over the top is excessive — too much, carried past the point anyone needed.

clue.text: Jury's findings after court's thrown out Italian scorer

indicators.note: Thrown out means got rid of, so the letters named are struck from the word they were sitting in.

parts.note: What a jury returns are its verdicts.
CT is the standard abbreviation for court and its apostrophe-s adds the S; those three letters are the ones that go.

explanation.surface: The jury's conclusions, arrived at after the court has thrown the case out.
explanation.walkthrough: Three letters leave, not two, because the apostrophe-s goes out with the abbreviation it is attached to. 'Scorer' is the setter's word for a composer, one who writes scores.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Verdi was the Italian composer of Aida and La traviata, so he scored for a living.

clue.text: Runners' trainers?

definitions.meaning: The surface offers athletes; a runner is also a climbing bean, the sort that needs something to climb.
Trainers reads as the shoes or the coaching staff; in a garden a trainer is whatever a plant is trained up.

explanation.surface: The footwear, or perhaps the coaching staff, belonging to a group of athletes.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words desert the running track for the vegetable patch, where runner beans are trained up a cane as they climb. The question mark is the only warning given.
explanation.definitionFit: Runner beans climb whatever is stood beside them, and a beanpole is the cane that does the training — the garden sense of both words at once.

clue.text: Badly bred, dined staying in PJs?

indicators.note: Something done badly is done wrong, and letters put together wrongly arrive in the wrong order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Someone of poor breeding who took dinner in their pyjamas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly bred' holds together as a phrase, which is exactly why the first word is easy to read past as insult rather than instruction. PJs are pyjamas.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody bedridden cannot get up at all, so pyjamas stay on all day — the clue's light way of saying confined to bed.

clue.text: Excess denim — rare — fancy!

indicators.note: To fancy something up is to work it into a different shape, and these letters are worked into another order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A delighted cry over a heap of leftover denim, rare stuff at that.
explanation.walkthrough: Four words separated by dashes, any of which could be the definition, and the punctuation gives nothing away. 'Fancy!' reads as surprise while quietly issuing the order.
explanation.definitionFit: A remainder is what is left over once the rest has gone — the excess of a print run or of a sum.

clue.text: Butcher's second wife unhappy

parts.note: A mo is a moment, the everyday British word for a second or two.
W is the standard abbreviation for wife.
Somebody unhappy is down.

explanation.surface: A butcher's second wife, in low spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second wife' holds together so naturally that it hides two separate pieces, and the butcher is a verb rather than the man behind the counter. A mo is a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: To butcher a body of men is to mow them down, killing indiscriminately and in numbers.

clue.text: Part of caterpillar going slowly

indicators.note: Part of something is a piece taken as it stands, its letters still in the order they were given.

parts.note: The run begins three letters from the end of the caterpillar and finishes two letters into the word behind it.

explanation.surface: A caterpillar making its way along at its own unhurried pace.
explanation.walkthrough: The hidden run needs both words, so 'going' is material rather than instruction — the temptation is to read it as the clue's verb. Largo is the marking at the slow end of a score.
explanation.definitionFit: Largo is the tempo direction telling a player to take the music slowly and broadly.

clue.text: Basic facts; a little conflict's arisen

indicators.note: in a down clue, something that has arisen has come up, so the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a tad is a little, a small amount
a war is a conflict

explanation.surface: A small dispute has broken out over the basic facts.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a down clue, so 'arisen' sends the whole phrase up the grid, reading it from the end. The 's after conflict is just 'is', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Raw data is unprocessed information, the basic facts and figures gathered before any analysis.

clue.text: Per Spooner, the time for gardening had come: no-one told me

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the N of the first word and the H of the last trade places, and the result is heard as a new phrase

parts.words: the time for gardening had come
parts.note: read as the phrase now was it to hoe: now is the time, and to hoe is a gardening job

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned announcement that planting season had arrived, said by someone blindsided.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'now was it to hoe' and, 'Per Spooner', swap the N and H sounds: you get 'how was it o-know', heard as 'how was I to know'.
explanation.definitionFit: How was I to know? is the exasperated protest of someone who was never told.

clue.text: Va-va-voom, or emphatically minimal speed?

indicators.note: Emphasis in speech comes of saying a thing twice over, so the letter it governs arrives doubled.

parts.note: The minimum on any speedometer is zero, written as the letter O, and said twice for emphasis: zero, zero.
MPH, miles per hour, is how speed is written on a British road sign.

explanation.surface: A word for zest, offered as an alternative to barely moving at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole answer is a stationary car read aloud: 00 mph. Va-va-voom reached Britain through Thierry Henry's Renault adverts, so both ends of the clue are motoring.
explanation.definitionFit: Oomph is energy, zest, allure — the va-va-voom something has when it is full of life.

clue.text: Change hearts of greedier visitors

indicators.note: The heart of a word is its middle, and the plural warns that more than one word is being opened up.

parts.note: Eight letters with a clean pair at the centre: gre|ed|ier.
Eight letters again, centred on this pair: vis|it|ors.

explanation.surface: Grasping house guests having a change of heart.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words run to eight letters, so each heart is a pair rather than a single letter. 'Change of heart' is the phrase the surface leans on while the clue means it literally.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit is to change a text — cut it, correct it, reshape it before it goes out.

clue.text: To begin with, thoroughbred turned, went at moderate pace

indicators.note: To begin with asks for the beginning of the word that follows, which is its opening letter and nothing more.

parts.note: The first letter of thoroughbred, taken off the front as the clue's opening words instruct.
Food that has turned has rotted.

explanation.surface: A racehorse turning and setting off at a steady pace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned' reads as a horse changing direction and means gone off, the way milk does. A trot is the gait between a walk and a canter, which is what makes the pace moderate.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse that trotted went at the moderate two-beat pace between walking and cantering.

clue.text: Mix using seeds to augment relish — delicious, primarily?

definitions.text: Mix using seeds to augment relish — delicious, primarily?

indicators.note: Primarily asks for what comes first, so each word in the run hands over only the letter it opens with.

parts.words: Mix using seeds to augment relish — delicious
parts.note: Seven words in order, each giving up its initial letter.

explanation.surface: A seed-based blend recommended for making the food it is served with taste better.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word works twice over: read straight the sentence describes the condiment, and read from the front letter by letter it spells it. 'Relish' is enjoyment here, not a rival sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: mustard is a paste ground from seeds, delicious, and eaten to heighten the relish of what it accompanies.

clue.text: Confines swans

definitions.note: The second definition is broader than the answer: a pen is specifically a female swan, so the clue names the bird rather than the sex.
definitions.meaning: Shuts livestock into an enclosure and keeps them there.
The female swan is a pen and the male a cob, a distinction swan-keepers still make.

explanation.surface: Shutting a flock of swans safely in for the night.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words and two unrelated senses: the verb for shutting animals up, and the keeper's name for the female bird. With nothing spelt out, the enumeration is all the help there is.
explanation.definitionFit: To pen animals is to confine them in an enclosure, and pens are the female swans on the water.

clue.text: Buff and shine statue, mostly vigorously

indicators.note: done vigorously, the letters are shaken hard into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

indicators.note: mostly means all but the last letter

parts.note: taken as written, then shortened
the last letter of statue, left off

explanation.surface: Someone instructed to polish a statue with real energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buff and shine' looks like a polishing job, but 'Buff' is the definition, a keen fan. 'Mostly' takes STATU from statue to go with SHINE.
explanation.definitionFit: A buff is an informed enthusiast, as in a film buff or history buff.
